pos: v. and n. (to run to the aid of one in distress; help brought in time; rendering Greek boetheo, Hebrew azar)
etymology: Latin succurrere, to run under, to run to help. The Greek of Hebrews 2 is the same picture — to run at a cry — and the runner is the tempted Christ.
biblical_def: “For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted” (Heb 2:18). Paul of the acceptable time: “in the day of salvation have I succoured thee” (2Co 6:2). Phebe was “a succourer of many, and of myself also” (Rom 16:2). The Syrians of Damascus “came to succour Hadadezer king of Zobah” (2Sa 8:5); David's men would not let him fight, for “now thou art worth ten thousand of us: therefore now it is better that thou succour us out of the city” (2Sa 18:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines succor as to help or relieve when in difficulty, want, or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering; and, as a noun, aid, help, assistance.
webster_full: SUCCOR, v.t. To help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering; as, to succor a besieged city; to succor prisoners.
SUCCOR, n. Aid; help; assistance; particularly, assistance that relieves and delivers from difficulty, want or distress.
scriptures: Heb 2:18
For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.
(For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)

But the people answered, Thou shalt not go forth: for if we flee away, they will not care for us; neither if half of us die, will they care for us: but now thou art worth ten thousand of us: therefore now it is better that thou succour us out of the city.
And when the Syrians of Damascus came to succour Hadadezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men.
corruption_summary: Christ's temptations are made a performance, and Hebrews grounds His power to succour on the fact that He suffered under them.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 2:18 will not let the temptation of Christ be a pageant. He suffered being tempted — the wilderness, Gethsemane, the whole life under the pressure of a sinless will against a world of solicitation — and because He suffered it He is able to succour, to run to the cry of, them that are tempted. A Christ who could not really be tempted could not really help; the succour is proportioned to the suffering. Chapter 4 completes the sentence: tempted in all points like as we are, yet without sin, and therefore a High Priest touched with the feeling of our infirmities. The Reformed doctrine of the impeccability of Christ — that He could not sin — has never meant that the temptation cost Him nothing; it cost Him blood in the garden. Second Corinthians 6:2 is succour's calendar: in the day of salvation have I succoured thee, and the day is now.
roots_summary: Greek boetheo (G997), to run to a cry, help; prostatis (G4368), a patroness, succourer; Hebrew azar (H5826), to help.
roots_lines: Greek boetheo (G997) — to succour, help; Hebrews 2:18, 2 Corinthians 6:2, Mark 9:22, 9:24.
Greek prostatis (G4368) — a succourer, patroness; Romans 16:2 only.
Hebrew azar (H5826) — to help, succour; 2 Samuel 8:5, 18:3, 1 Chronicles 18:5.
usage: “In that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted” — succour proportioned to suffering.
“In the day of salvation have I succoured thee” — and the day is now.
“A succourer of many, and of myself also” — Phebe.

pos: adv. and prep. (beneath, below; rendering Hebrew tachath and lematah)
etymology: Under + neath, Old English neothan, below. Moses' last blessing puts the everlasting arms in the one place a falling man needs them.
biblical_def: Moses' blessing on Israel: “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them” (Deu 33:27). Of the ephod: “two other rings of gold thou shalt make, and shalt put them on the two sides of the ephod underneath, toward the forepart thereof” (Exo 28:27), and so they made them (Exo 39:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines underneath as beneath; below; in a lower place.
webster_full: UNDERNEATH, adv. Beneath; below; in a lower place.
UNDERNEATH, prep. Under; beneath.
scriptures: The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.

And two other rings of gold thou shalt make, and shalt put them on the two sides of the ephod underneath, toward the forepart thereof, over against the other coupling thereof, above the curious girdle of the ephod.
And they made two other golden rings, and put them on the two sides of the ephod underneath, toward the forepart of it, over against the other coupling thereof, above the curious girdle of the ephod.
corruption_summary: God is placed above the believer as an aspiration, and Moses put the everlasting arms underneath him as a floor.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 33:27 is the last thing Moses said about God before he went up to die, and its preposition is the doctrine. Not above, where the aspiring reach and never arrive; not beside, where the companionable God of the modern hymn walks along; but underneath — the everlasting arms are where a man goes when he falls, and he cannot fall through them. The verse has two halves and the church keeps one: the arms underneath, and the enemy thrust out from before, with the word Destroy. Refuge and warfare are one blessing. The rings underneath the ephod are the small picture of the same truth — the breastplate with the twelve names was held to the priest's heart by rings fastened out of sight, beneath, and the people's names did not fall off because of what was under them.
roots_lines: Hebrew mittachat (H8478) — from beneath, underneath; Deuteronomy 33:27.
Hebrew millematah (H4295) — from beneath, underneath; Exodus 28:27, 39:20.
usage: “The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms” — the floor a man cannot fall through.
“He shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them” — the half the church forgets.
“On the two sides of the ephod underneath” — the rings out of sight that held the names.

pos: n. and v. (a retinue; the trailing skirt of a robe; to bring up, to dedicate; rendering Hebrew chayil, shul, and chanak)
etymology: Old French trainer, to drag. The Hebrew of Proverbs 22 is to dedicate — the verb of the dedication of a house and of the temple — and the Hebrew of Isaiah 6 is the hem of a garment.
biblical_def: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). “In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple” (Isa 6:1). The queen of Sheba “came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones” (1Ki 10:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines train as that which is drawn along behind; the tail of a gown; a retinue; and, as a verb, to draw along; to educate; to bring up; to form by instruction.
webster_full: TRAIN, n. That which is drawn along behind; the trailing part of a gown; the tail of a bird.
2. A retinue; a number of followers or attendants.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along.
2. To educate; to teach; to form by instruction or practice; to bring up.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Isa 6:1
In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.

And she came to Jerusalem with a very great train, with camels that bare spices, and very much gold, and precious stones: and when she was come to Solomon, she communed with him of all that was in her heart.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 22:6 is read as a guarantee and as a licence to follow the child's bent, and the Hebrew verb is to dedicate.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misreadings meet in Proverbs 22:6. The first takes it as a promise with a warranty, so that a prodigal proves a failed parent; it is a proverb, the shape of God's ordinary government, and the man who trained Absalom wrote psalms. The second is newer: the way he should go is read as the child's own bent, his personality, his inclination, so that training means following the child. The Hebrew verb is chanak, to dedicate — the word for the dedication of the temple and of a house — and a dedication is not a discovery of what the thing wants but a setting apart of it for God. Train up a child is: dedicate the child, put him on the way, and the way in Proverbs is always the fear of the LORD. Isaiah's train is the other word, and it is the hem: the skirt of the Lord's robe filled the temple, which means the smallest and lowest part of His glory was more than the house could hold.
roots_summary: Hebrew chanak (H2596), to dedicate, initiate, train; shul (H7757), the skirt, hem, train; chayil (H2428), a company, retinue.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to dedicate, train; Proverbs 22:6, Deuteronomy 20:5, 1 Kings 8:63.
Hebrew shul (H7757) — skirt, train; Isaiah 6:1, Exodus 28:33–34.
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — a company, train; 1 Kings 10:2, 2 Chronicles 9:1.
usage: “Train up a child in the way he should go” — the verb is dedicate.
“His train filled the temple” — the hem alone, and the house could not hold it.
“A very great train” — the queen of Sheba's retinue.

pos: v. (past participle of win: gained, brought over; rendering Greek kerdaino, Hebrew shalal)
etymology: Old English winnan, to labour, strive, and so to gain by striving. Peter's Greek is the merchant's gain, the word the Lord uses for gaining a brother.
biblical_def: “Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives; While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear” (1Pe 3:1–2). “A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle” (Pro 18:19). The captains dedicated “out of the spoils won in battles… to maintain the house of the LORD” (1Ch 26:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives won as the past tense and participle of win: gained, obtained by effort, brought over.
webster_full: WON, pret. and pp. of win. Gained; obtained; procured; prevailed on; brought over.
scriptures: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives;
A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle.
Out of the spoils won in battles did they dedicate to maintain the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Without the word is read as never mentioning the gospel, and Peter's wife wins by a life the gospel has already changed.
corruption_paragraphs: First Peter 3:1 is addressed to a wife whose husband obeys not the word — he has heard it and will not have it — and it tells her how such a man is won: not by the word again, which he has refused, but by the conversation of the wife, her conduct, chaste and coupled with fear. The verse is misread two ways. The feminist reads subjection as the problem; Peter makes it the instrument. The timid reads without the word as a rule of silence about Christ; it is a statement about what will finally move a man who has stopped listening, and it is not silence but a life that argues while the mouth rests. The order of the passage is complementarian to the end: the wife wins by being what the word has made her, and the husband is told in verse 7 what his own conduct costs him if he fails — his prayers hindered. Proverbs 18:19 is the difficulty of the same winning in another relation: a brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city, and the winning is worth the siege.
roots_summary: Greek kerdaino (G2770), to gain, win; Hebrew shalal (H7998), spoil, plunder won.
roots_lines: Greek kerdaino (G2770) — to gain, win; 1 Peter 3:1, Matthew 18:15, 1 Corinthians 9:19–22, Philippians 3:8.
Hebrew shalal (H7998) — spoil, spoils won; 1 Chronicles 26:27; Proverbs 18:19 supplies the verb.
usage: “They also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives” — a life that argues while the mouth rests.
“A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city” — the siege worth laying.
“Out of the spoils won in battles” — dedicated to the house.

pos: v. (to roll about, in ashes or in mire; rendering Hebrew palash and saphaq, Greek kulio and kulisma)
etymology: Old English wealwian, to roll. The prophets wallow in ashes for repentance; Peter's sow wallows in mire because it is a sow.
biblical_def: Jeremiah: “O daughter of my people, gird thee with sackcloth, and wallow thyself in ashes: make thee mourning, as for an only son” (Jer 6:26); to the shepherds, “Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock” (Jer 25:34); of Moab, “Make ye him drunken: for he magnified himself against the LORD: Moab also shall wallow in his vomit” (Jer 48:26). The boy in Mark “fell on the ground, and wallowed foaming” (Mar 9:20). And Peter's proverb: “The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire” (2Pe 2:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wallow as to roll one's body on the earth, in mire, or on other substance; to move heavily and clumsily; to live in filth or gross vice.
webster_full: WALLOW, v.i. To roll one's body on the earth, in mire, or on other substance; to tumble and roll in water.
2. To move heavily and clumsily.
3. To live in filth or gross vice.
scriptures: But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.
Jer 6:26
O daughter of my people, gird thee with sackcloth, and wallow thyself in ashes: make thee mourning, as for an only son, most bitter lamentation: for the spoiler shall suddenly come upon us.
Make ye him drunken: for he magnified himself against the LORD: Moab also shall wallow in his vomit, and he also shall be in derision.
Mar 9:20
And they brought him unto him: and when he saw him, straightway the spirit tare him; and he fell on the ground, and wallowed foaming.

Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel.
corruption_summary: Reformation is mistaken for regeneration, and Peter's sow was washed and went back to the mire because washing does not change a sow.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Peter 2:22 is the Bible's own explanation of the apostate, and it is about nature. The sow was washed — really washed, clean, dry, presentable — and she returned to her wallowing in the mire, not because the washing failed but because nothing had been done to the sow. A reformed life without a renewed heart is a washed pig, and the mire is a question of time. The verse stands against every doctrine of conversion that changes conduct and leaves the creature: the man who was sober, moral, and churchgoing and went back is the sow, and his return is the proof of what he always was. Jeremiah's wallowing is the opposite creature in the opposite substance: the daughter of Zion wallowing in ashes, the shepherds in ashes, mourning as for an only son — repentance rolling in what it deserves. Between the ashes and the mire is the whole difference between a sinner and a sow.
roots_summary: Hebrew palash (H6428), to roll in ashes; saphaq (H5606), to splash, wallow; Greek kulio (G2947), to roll; kulisma (G2946), a wallowing place.
roots_lines: Hebrew palash, hithpael (H6428) — to wallow, roll in ashes; Jeremiah 6:26, 25:34, Ezekiel 27:30, Micah 1:10.
Hebrew saphaq (H5606) — to wallow, splash; Jeremiah 48:26.
Greek kulio (G2947) — to roll, wallow; Mark 9:20; kulisma (G2946), 2 Peter 2:22.
usage: “The sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire” — washing does not change a sow.
“Wallow thyself in ashes: make thee mourning, as for an only son” — repentance rolling in what it deserves.
“Moab also shall wallow in his vomit” — for magnifying himself against the LORD.

pos: v. (fascinated, brought under a spell; rendering Greek baskaino and existemi)
etymology: Be + witch, Old English wicce. Paul's Greek is the evil eye — to fascinate by a look — and he asks the Galatians who has done it to them.
biblical_def: “O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?” (Gal 3:1). Simon in Samaria “used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one” (Act 8:9), and “of long time he had bewitched them with sorceries” (Act 8:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bewitch as to fascinate; to gain an ascendancy over by charms or incantation; to charm; to please to such a degree as to take away the power of resistance.
webster_full: BEWITCH, v.t. To fascinate; to gain an ascendancy over by charms or incantation; an operation which was formerly supposed to injure the person bewitched.
2. To charm; to fascinate; to please to such a degree as to take away the power of resistance.
scriptures: Gal 3:1
O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?
Act 8:9
But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one:
Act 8:11
And to him they had regard, because that of long time he had bewitched them with sorceries.
corruption_summary: Legalism is thought to be a sober error, and Paul calls it a spell cast on people who had seen Christ crucified.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not argue with the Galatians in 3:1; he asks who put the spell on them. They had seen Christ crucified set forth before their eyes — the preaching had been that vivid — and they were now looking at circumcision as the thing that would make them right, and the only explanation the apostle can find is the evil eye. Legalism is not the sober, cautious error the modern church takes it for; it is a fascination, a look away from the cross toward something the man can do, and it works on people who know better. The question that follows is the cure: received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith? Simon's bewitching of Samaria is the pagan form, a sorcerer with a city under his charm, giving out that himself was some great one — and the charm broke when Philip preached, which is how every bewitching breaks.
roots_summary: Greek baskaino (G940), to fascinate with the evil eye, bewitch; existemi (G1839), to put out of one's senses, amaze, bewitch.
roots_lines: Greek baskaino (G940) — to bewitch, fascinate; Galatians 3:1 only.
Greek existemi (G1839) — to amaze, bewitch; Acts 8:9, 8:11, 8:13.
usage: “Who hath bewitched you… before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified” — legalism as a spell.
“Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?” — the cure.
“Bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one” — Simon.

pos: adj. (not subject to decay; imperishable; rendering Greek aphthartos)
etymology: Latin in + corrumpere, to break up. The Greek aphthartos is undecaying, and Peter uses it of a seed, an inheritance, and God.
biblical_def: “Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever” (1Pe 1:23). “To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you” (1Pe 1:4). “The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1Co 15:52). The athlete strives for a corruptible crown, “but we an incorruptible” (1Co 9:25). And the Gentiles “changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image” (Rom 1:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incorruptible as that cannot be corrupted; that cannot decay or perish; that cannot be bribed; inflexibly just and upright.
webster_full: INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot be corrupted; that cannot decay or perish; as, the incorruptible bodies of the saints after the resurrection.
2. That cannot be bribed; inflexibly just and upright.
scriptures: Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
Rom 1:23
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.
corruption_summary: Regeneration is attributed to water, and Peter says the incorruptible seed is the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: First Peter 1:23 names the seed of the new birth, and it is not a sacrament. Born again, not of corruptible seed but of incorruptible, by the word of God — the word preached, Peter says two verses later, the gospel that was preached unto you. Regeneration comes by the Spirit through the Word, and every doctrine that locates it in the font has changed the seed. The seed is called incorruptible because what it produces cannot die: the life begotten by an undecaying word is itself undecaying, which is why the same letter can promise an inheritance incorruptible, reserved in heaven, to people who were about to be persecuted out of everything corruptible they owned. First Corinthians 15:52 is the seed's harvest, the dead raised incorruptible — the body, not a ghost — and Romans 1:23 the word's warning: men exchanged the glory of the uncorruptible God for images of things that rot.
roots_lines: Greek aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible; Romans 1:23, 1 Corinthians 9:25, 15:52, 1 Timothy 1:17, 1 Peter 1:4, 1:23, 3:4.
usage: “Born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God” — the seed named, and it is not water.
“An inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away” — promised to people about to lose everything else.
“The dead shall be raised incorruptible” — the body.

pos: n. (relative measure; in Romans 12, the rule by which prophecy is measured; rendering Greek analogia, Hebrew erek and ma'ar)
etymology: Latin proportio, comparative relation. The Greek of Romans 12:6, analogia, occurs once in the New Testament and gave theology its phrase, the analogy of faith.
biblical_def: “Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith” (Rom 12:6). Of leviathan: “I will not conceal his parts, nor his power, nor his comely proportion” (Job 41:12). Of Solomon's bases: “cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one” (1Ki 7:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines proportion as the comparative relation of one thing to another; the relation which one part bears to another or to the whole; symmetry; a due measure.
webster_full: PROPORTION, n. The comparative relation of one thing to another; the relation or adaptation of one portion to another, or to the whole, as respects magnitude, quantity or degree.
2. Symmetry; suitable adaptation of one part or thing to another.
3. Equal or just share; lot; a due measure.
scriptures: Rom 12:6
Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith;
I will not conceal his parts, nor his power, nor his comely proportion.
For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about.
corruption_summary: Prophecy is claimed as new revelation, and Paul bound it to the proportion of faith, which is the rule the church calls the analogy of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 12:6 gives prophecy a measure, and the measure is not the prophet's confidence. Let us prophesy according to the proportion — the analogia — of faith: in agreement with the faith once delivered, the body of truth against which every utterance in the church is to be checked. The Reformers took the phrase and made it a rule of interpretation, the analogy of faith, by which no text is read against the plain teaching of the whole, and no prophet is heard against the apostles. The charismatic claim to words from God that add to Scripture fails this verse before it fails any other: a prophecy out of proportion to the faith is not a higher word but a false one, and Paul's other rule, in 1 Corinthians 14, is that the prophets are to be judged. Job's leviathan has a comely proportion, and Solomon's bases were graven according to the proportion of every one — the word means a thing measured to its place, and that is what a word in the church must be.
roots_summary: Greek analogia (G356), proportion, analogy; Hebrew erek (H6187), arrangement, order; ma'ar (H4626), proportion, bare space.
roots_lines: Greek analogia (G356) — proportion, analogy; Romans 12:6 only.
Hebrew erek (H6187) — arrangement, comely proportion; Job 41:12; ma'ar (H4626), 1 Kings 7:36.
usage: “Let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith” — the rule the church named after it.
“His comely proportion” — leviathan, measured to his place.
“According to the proportion of every one” — Solomon's graven bases.

pos: n. (a show put forward to cover a purpose; rendering Greek prophasis)
etymology: Latin praetendere, to stretch before. The Greek prophasis is a thing shown in front — the long prayer in front of the widow's house.
biblical_def: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation” (Mat 23:14; Mar 12:40). And Paul in prison: “What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice” (Php 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pretense as a holding out or offering to others something false or feigned; a false show; assumption of that which is not real or true.
webster_full: PRETENSE, n. A holding out or offering to others something false or feigned; a presenting to others, either in words or actions, a false or hypocritical appearance, usually with a view to conceal what is real, and thus to deceive.
2. Assumption; claim to notice.
3. Claim, true or false.
scriptures: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation.
Which devour widows' houses, and for a pretence make long prayers: these shall receive greater damnation.
Php 1:18
What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.
corruption_summary: Long prayers cover the devouring of widows' houses, and Paul rejoiced that Christ was preached even by men whose motive was a pretence.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:14 is the Lord's word for the religious fraud: the long prayer as a pretence, a thing put in front of the widow's house while the house is devoured behind it. The verse is exact about the sequence — the devouring is the purpose, the praying is the cover — and about the sentence, the greater damnation, because the fraud has used God as the disguise. Every ministry that lives on the gifts of the poor and old while performing its devotion for them has this verse for its epitaph. Philippians 1:18 is the word's surprising other use. Some preached Christ of envy and strife, hoping to add affliction to Paul's bonds, and Paul's verdict was that Christ was preached, in pretence or in truth, and he rejoiced. The gospel's power does not depend on the preacher's heart; the message saves whether the messenger is sincere or not, which is the answer to Donatus and a comfort to every congregation that has since discovered what its minister was.
roots_summary: Greek prophasis (G4392), a pretext, a show put forward, pretence.
roots_lines: Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretence, pretext, cloke; Matthew 23:14, Mark 12:40, Luke 20:47, Philippians 1:18, John 15:22, 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
usage: “For a pretence make long prayer” — the devotion in front of the devouring.
“Ye shall receive the greater damnation” — because God was the disguise.
“Whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice” — the message saves regardless of the messenger.

pos: v. (to be in debt; to be bound to pay or render; rendering Greek opheilo and prosopheilo)
etymology: Old English āgan, to own, to have; to owe was first to have as an obligation. The Greek opheilo is both the debtor's word and the word for a duty.
biblical_def: “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law” (Rom 13:8). The forgiven servant found his fellow “which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest” (Mat 18:28), having himself owed ten thousand talents (Mat 18:24). “There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty” (Luk 7:41). The unjust steward: “How much owest thou unto my lord?” (Luk 16:5). Paul to Philemon: “albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides” (Phm 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines owe as to be indebted; to be obliged or bound to pay; to be obliged to ascribe to; to be due or owing.
webster_full: OWE, v.t. To be indebted; to be obliged or bound to pay.
2. To be obliged to ascribe to; to be obliged for; as, that he may owe to me all his deliverance.
3. To possess; to have; to be the owner of. Obsolete.
scriptures: Rom 13:8
Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest.
And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents.
Luk 7:41
There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.
Phm 1:19
I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.
corruption_summary: The forgiven demand payment of what is owed them, and the parable's ten thousand talents are set against the hundred pence for exactly that man.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 18 is the arithmetic of forgiveness. A servant owed ten thousand talents — a sum no life could repay — and was forgiven the whole of it on a plea; he went out and found a man who owed him a hundred pence and took him by the throat. The Lord told the story to Peter, who had asked how often he must forgive, and the point is the ratio: what any man is owed by another is a hundred pence against the ten thousand talents he has been forgiven, and the one who cannot see the ratio has not understood what was done for him. The end of the parable is the end of the unforgiving. Romans 13:8 is the one debt Scripture leaves standing: owe no man any thing, but to love one another — a debt paid every day and never paid off. Paul's line to Philemon is the pastor's version of the same ledger: thou owest unto me even thine own self — which he mentions only to say he will not mention it.
roots_summary: Greek opheilo (G3784), to owe, be indebted, be bound; prosopheilo (G4359), to owe besides; opheiletes (G3781), a debtor.
roots_lines: Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe; Romans 13:8, Matthew 18:28, Luke 7:41, 16:5, Philemon 1:18.
Greek prosopheilo (G4359) — to owe besides; Philemon 1:19 only; opheiletes (G3781), a debtor; Matthew 18:24.
usage: “Pay me that thou owest” — a hundred pence, from a man forgiven ten thousand talents.
“Owe no man any thing, but to love one another” — the debt paid daily and never paid off.
“Thou owest unto me even thine own self besides” — mentioned only to be waived.
